ch38.title: Jerusalem at the Feast of Tabernacles
ch38.b001: A Village on the Slopes of Gilboa
ch38.b002: Jesus set out for Jerusalem with the ten apostles by way of Samaria, the shorter route. They went down the eastern shore of the lake and through Scythopolis into the borders of Samaria, and near nightfall Jesus sent Philip and Matthew to a village on the eastern slopes of Mount Gilboa to find lodging. These villagers were even more prejudiced against the Jews than most Samaritans, and their feelings ran high just then, with so many pilgrims passing on their way to the feast of tabernacles. They knew little of Jesus, and they refused him lodging because he was a Jew. When Matthew and Philip indignantly told them that they were turning away the Holy One of Israel, the infuriated villagers chased the two out of town with sticks and stones.
ch38.b003: When James and John heard the report, they stepped up to Jesus: “⟦Q 162:0.2⟧Master, we pray you to give us permission to bid fire come down from heaven to devour these insolent and impenitent Samaritans.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus turned upon the sons of Zebedee and severely rebuked them: “⟦Q 162:0.2⟧You know not what manner of attitude you manifest. Vengeance savors not of the outlook of the kingdom of heaven. Rather than dispute, let us journey over to the little village by the Jordan ford.⟦/Q⟧” So, because of sectarian prejudice, those Samaritans denied themselves the honor of showing hospitality to the Creator Son of a universe. The company spent the night by the ford, crossed the river in the morning, and went on by the east Jordan highway, arriving at Bethany late on Wednesday evening. Thomas and Nathaniel, delayed by Rodan, came on Friday.
ch38.b005: For a long time Jesus’ followers had begged him to go to Jerusalem and preach at the center of Jewish learning, and to every plea he had answered, “⟦Q 162:1.1⟧The hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧” Now that the Sanhedrin wanted him for trial and he himself had lately spoken again and again of his death, the apostles were stunned by his sudden decision to attend the feast. To their protests of fear he answered only, “But the hour has come.” In spite of all their efforts to dissuade him, he went boldly into the city several times during the feast and taught publicly in the temple. Many disciples, and even Judas Iscariot, had dared to think that he had fled to Phoenicia out of fear of the Jewish leaders and Herod Antipas. His appearance in Jerusalem put an end forever to all such whisperings about fear and cowardice.
ch38.b006: There were reasons why he could teach in the temple courts and live to go away. Many members of the Sanhedrin secretly believed in him or were unwilling to arrest him during the feast, with the city full of pilgrims friendly to his cause. The labors of Abner and his associates throughout Judea had also turned sentiment toward the kingdom. Above all, his audacity overawed his enemies. They supposed he must have been promised protection by the Romans, perhaps through Philip, Herod Antipas’s brother, who was almost a follower. One or two months earlier he would certainly have been put to death. Thousands of believers from all parts of the Roman Empire saw him, heard him teach, and many came out to Bethany to talk with him about the kingdom in their home lands. Yet every time he went into the city his apostles were filled with terror, all the more as his pronouncements about his mission grew bolder day by day.
ch38.b007: The First Teaching in the Temple
ch38.b008: On the first afternoon that Jesus taught in the temple, a curious listener interrupted to ask how he could quote the Scriptures and teach so fluently when he had never studied with the rabbis. Jesus replied: “⟦Q 162:2.1⟧No man has taught me the truths which I declare to you. And this teaching is not mine but His who sent me. If any man really desires to do my Father’s will, he shall certainly know about my teaching, whether it be God’s or whether I speak for myself.⟦/Q⟧” Moses had commanded, “You shall not kill,” yet some of them sought to kill the Son of Man. When someone asked why the rulers wanted to kill him, he answered that they resented a gospel that set men free from the burdensome traditions of a religion of ceremonies; they circumcised on the Sabbath but would kill him for making a man whole on the Sabbath. “⟦Q 162:2.2⟧And now do I appeal to every one of you: Judge not according to outward appearances but rather judge by the true spirit of these teachings; judge righteously.⟦/Q⟧”
ch38.b009: The crowd fell to wrangling. Some said he was mad, some that he had a devil, others that this was the prophet of Galilee whom the scribes had long sought to kill. The Pharisees resolved to stop his appearances, and Eber, the proper officer of the Sanhedrin, was sent with two assistants to arrest him. As Eber approached, the Master said: “⟦Q 162:2.6⟧Fear not to approach me. Draw near while you listen to my teaching. I know you have been sent to apprehend me, but you should understand that nothing will befall the Son of Man until his hour comes.⟦/Q⟧” He bore none of them ill will, he said; the Father loved them. “⟦Q 162:2.7⟧If you could only realize that I am to be with you only a little while! In just a short time I go to Him who sent me into this world.… for where I am about to go you cannot come.⟦/Q⟧”
ch38.b010: Eber and his assistants went back without him. When the chief priests and Pharisees upbraided them, Eber replied: “⟦Q 162:2.9⟧We feared to arrest him in the midst of the multitude because many believe in him. Besides, we never heard a man speak like this man.⟦/Q⟧” The rulers taunted him: was he also led astray? Eber answered: “⟦Q 162:2.9⟧Even so, my masters, but this man speaks to the multitude words of mercy and hope.… And even then does not our law require fairness? Do we condemn a man before we hear him?⟦/Q⟧” The chief of the Sanhedrin turned on him in anger: “⟦Q 162:2.9⟧Have you gone mad? Are you by any chance also from Galilee? Search the Scriptures, and you will discover that out of Galilee arises no prophet, much less the Messiah.⟦/Q⟧” The Sanhedrin broke up in confusion, and Jesus withdrew to Bethany for the night.
ch38.b012: Early on the third morning of the feast, as Jesus approached the temple, a group of the Sanhedrin’s hired agents met him, dragging a woman. Their spokesman said: “⟦Q 162:3.2⟧Master, this woman was taken in adultery—in the very act. Now, the law of Moses commands that we should stone such a woman. What do you say should be done with her?⟦/Q⟧” It was a snare. If he upheld the law, he would be in trouble with Rome, which had denied the Jews the right to inflict death without a Roman tribunal; if he forbade the stoning, they would accuse him of setting himself above Moses; if he kept silent, they would call him a coward. Later accounts would make it seem that the scribes and Pharisees brought her and were themselves shamed, but they, for all their blindness, were among the most thoroughly moral men of their day.
ch38.b013: The truth was more sordid. The woman, once comely, was the wife of an inferior citizen of Nazareth who had been a troublemaker for Jesus throughout his youth. This man forced his wife to earn their living by making commerce of her body, and he had struck a bargain with the hirelings of the rulers to betray her, so that they might ensnare Jesus. Looking over the crowd, Jesus saw the husband standing behind the others and knew him for a party to the scheme. He walked over near him and wrote a few words in the sand, and the man departed in haste. Then he came back and wrote again on the ground for the accusers, and when they read it, they too went away, one by one. When he wrote a third time, the woman’s companion in evil left as well. Jesus raised himself up and saw her standing alone. “⟦Q 162:3.5⟧Woman, where are your accusers? did no man remain to stone you?⟦/Q⟧” She lifted her eyes: “No man, Lord.” And Jesus said: “⟦Q 162:3.5⟧I know about you; neither do I condemn you. Go your way in peace.⟦/Q⟧” This woman, Hildana, forsook her wicked husband and joined the disciples of the kingdom.
ch38.b015: People had come from all the known world, from Spain to India. It was the feast of the harvest ingathering, held in the cool of autumn, and the pilgrims lived much in the open air, in leafy booths. Levitical chants rang out amid the solemn blasts of the priests’ silvery trumpets, and at night the temple and its throngs were brilliantly lit by the great candelabras in the court of the women and the glare of scores of torches. The whole city was gaily decorated, except the Roman castle of Antonia, which looked down in grim contrast. Each morning a priest bore a golden pitcher in procession to the pool of Siloam, and back in the temple the water and the wine of the drink offering were poured into silver funnels at the base of the altar, a rite that symbolized the outpouring of the divine spirit.
ch38.b016: On the evening before the last day, when the candelabras and torches were blazing, Jesus stood up in the midst of the throng and said: “⟦Q 162:5.2⟧I am the light of the world. He who follows me shall not walk in darkness but shall have the light of life.⟦/Q⟧” To those who said that witness to himself could not be true, he replied that he knew whence he came, who he was, and whither he went, and that his Father bore witness with him. “⟦Q 162:5.4⟧When the Son of Man is lifted up, then shall you all know that I am he, and that I have done nothing of myself but only as the Father has taught me.⟦/Q⟧” Many believed, and no man dared to lay hands upon him.
ch38.b017: On the last day, the great day of the feast, just after the procession from Siloam had passed and the priests had poured the water and the wine upon the altar, while the people paused after chanting the Hallel and the sacrifices were being prepared, the pilgrims heard the Master’s voice: “⟦Q 162:6.1⟧If any man thirst, let him come to me and drink. From the Father above I bring to this world the water of life. He who believes me shall be filled with the spirit which this water represents, for even the Scriptures have said, ‘Out of him shall flow rivers of living waters.’ When the Son of Man has finished his work on earth, there shall be poured out upon all flesh the living Spirit of Truth. Those who receive this spirit shall never know spiritual thirst.⟦/Q⟧”
ch38.b019: That afternoon, after the apostles had failed to persuade him to flee the city, Jesus went once more to teach in Solomon’s Porch. To the believers gathered there he said: “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧If my words abide in you and you are minded to do the will of my Father, then are you truly my disciples. You shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.⟦/Q⟧” He spoke not of freedom from outward rule but of the liberties of the soul: “⟦Q 162:7.2⟧Verily, verily, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is the bond servant of sin.… If, therefore, the Son shall make you free, shall make you sons, you shall be free indeed.⟦/Q⟧”
ch38.b020: When he said that whoever kept his word of truth alive in his heart would never taste death, a scribe at his side declared that this proved he had a devil, for Abraham and the prophets were dead. Jesus answered that it was the Father who would glorify him, and that “⟦Q 162:7.5⟧even Abraham rejoiced to see my day, and by faith he saw it and was glad.⟦/Q⟧” The unbelievers and the agents of the Sanhedrin raised a tumult: “⟦Q 162:7.6⟧You are not fifty years of age, and yet you talk about seeing Abraham; you are a child of the devil!⟦/Q⟧” Jesus could not go on. He said only, as he departed, “⟦Q 162:7.6⟧Verily, verily, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.⟦/Q⟧” Many rushed off for stones, and the agents tried to seize him, but the Master made his way quickly through the temple corridors and escaped to a secret meeting place near Bethany, where Martha, Mary, and Lazarus were waiting for him.
ch38.b022: Because the authorities were again growing bold, it had been arranged that Jesus should lodge with Lazarus and his sisters at a friend’s house, while the apostles scattered in small groups. For years it had been the custom of these three to drop everything and listen whenever Jesus came. Since their parents’ death Martha had carried the household, and that evening, while Lazarus and Mary sat at Jesus’ feet drinking in his teaching, she busied herself with the meal. It was her disposition to be distracted by needless tasks and cumbered with trivial cares, and as she hurried about she grew vexed that Mary did nothing to help.
ch38.b023: At last she went to Jesus: “⟦Q 162:8.3⟧Master, do you not care that my sister has left me alone to do all of the serving? Will you not bid her to come and help me?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered: “⟦Q 162:8.3⟧Martha, Martha, why are you always anxious about so many things and troubled by so many trifles? Only one thing is really worth while, and since Mary has chosen this good and needful part, I shall not take it away from her. But when will both of you learn to live as I have taught you: both serving in co-operation and both refreshing your souls in unison? Can you not learn that there is a time for everything—that the lesser matters of life should give way before the greater things of the heavenly kingdom?⟦/Q⟧”
ch38.b025: The day after the feast ended Jesus left for Bethany, and he did not teach in the temple again during this visit. While the twelve instructed scores of believers at Bethany, he worked with Abner, who now had his headquarters at Bethlehem and had sent workers through Judea, southern Samaria, and even to Alexandria. Jesus and Abner arranged to unite the work of the two apostolic groups. The courage Jesus had shown in Jerusalem and the sympathetic understanding of his private teaching at Bethlehem won over each of John’s former apostles to a wholehearted acceptance of the kingdom. Early in November Abner and his eleven fellows cast their lot with Jesus and the twelve and labored with them as one organization right on down to the crucifixion.
ch38.b026: On Sunday, October 30, after a few days of rest in seclusion at the city of Ephraim, Jesus and the twelve went north by the west Jordan highway and reached Magadan Park late on Wednesday afternoon, November 2. The apostles were greatly relieved to have their Master back on friendly soil. No more did they urge him to go up to Jerusalem to proclaim the gospel of the kingdom.
ch39.title: The Seventy and the Good Samaritan
ch39.b001: By the Lake at Magadan, November 19
ch39.b002: A few days after Jesus returned from Jerusalem, Abner arrived from Bethlehem with some fifty disciples. Gathered at Magadan Camp were also the evangelistic corps, the women’s corps, and about a hundred and fifty other tried disciples from all over Palestine. From Friday, November 4, to the Sabbath of November 19, Jesus and the twelve gave this company a course of intensive training. Jesus spoke to them each morning; Peter taught methods of public preaching, Nathaniel the art of teaching, Thomas how to answer questions, and Matthew the ordering of group finances.
ch39.b003: About two o’clock on that Sabbath afternoon, between showers of rain, more than four hundred believers, David and most of his messengers among them, gathered on the shore of the lake to witness the ordination of the seventy: Abner and ten of John’s former apostles, fifty-one of the earlier evangelists, and eight other disciples who had distinguished themselves. Before laying his hands on them, Jesus said: “⟦Q 163:1.3⟧The harvest is indeed plenteous, but the laborers are few; therefore I exhort all of you to pray that the Lord of the harvest will send still other laborers into his harvest. I am about to set you apart as messengers of the kingdom; I am about to send you to Jew and gentile as lambs among wolves.⟦/Q⟧” They were to go two and two, carrying neither purse nor extra clothing; on entering a home they were first to say, “Peace be to this household,” and they were not to move from house to house for better lodging. “Remember, as you go forth proclaiming peace on earth and good will among men, you must contend with bitter and self-deceived enemies; therefore be as wise as serpents while you are also as harmless as doves.
ch39.b004: “⟦Q 163:1.4⟧And everywhere you go, preach, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is at hand,’ and minister to all who may be sick in either mind or body. Freely you have received of the good things of the kingdom; freely give.… He who hears you hears me. And he who hears me hears Him who sent me.⟦/Q⟧”
ch39.b005: Then, as they knelt in a circle about him, he began with Abner and laid his hands upon the head of every man. Early the next morning Abner sent the thirty-five couples out into all the cities of Galilee, Samaria, and Judea.
ch39.b006: The Young Man Who Went Away Sorrowful
ch39.b007: More than fifty others had sought a place among the seventy. A committee of Andrew, Abner, and the acting head of the evangelists had judged the candidates, bringing doubtful cases to Jesus. The Master never rejected anyone who craved ordination, but more than a dozen, after talking with him, no longer wished it. To one who asked leave first to bury his aged father, Jesus said: “⟦Q 163:2.2⟧My son, the foxes have holes, and the birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.⟦/Q⟧” He could remain a faithful disciple and minister to his loved ones, but the messengers must let others bury the dead. To another who wished first to comfort his family, he said: “⟦Q 163:2.3⟧No man, having put his hand to the plough, if he turns back, is worthy to become a messenger of the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧”
ch39.b008: Then Andrew brought a rich young man, a devout believer named Matadormus, a member of the Jerusalem Sanhedrin. Early the next morning, as Jesus went out for a walk, the young man accosted him: he had kept all the commandments from his youth; what more must he do to gain eternal life? Jesus answered that salvation is the reward of faith, not merely of works, and since Matadormus believed the gospel, “⟦Q 163:2.4⟧Then are you indeed my disciple and a child of the kingdom.⟦/Q⟧” But the young man was not content to be a disciple; he wanted to be one of the new messengers. Jesus looked down upon him with great love, and, kissing the kneeling young man on the forehead, said: “⟦Q 163:2.5⟧If you would be my messenger, go and sell all that you have and, when you have bestowed the proceeds upon the poor or upon your brethren, come and follow me, and you shall have treasure in the kingdom of heaven.⟦/Q⟧”
ch39.b009: At this the young man’s countenance fell. He arose and went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. He had been raised to believe that wealth was the token of God’s favor, and Jesus knew he was not free from the love of himself and his riches. The Master wanted to deliver him from the love of wealth, not necessarily from the wealth; only the apostles and the seventy, who lived with him as one family, gave up all their goods. Years later, after the church was established at Jerusalem, Matadormus did as the Master had asked and became treasurer of the Jerusalem church under James, the Lord’s brother. But it was then too late to be one of the seventy, and he had lost the intimate association with the Master that might have been his.
ch39.b010: Jesus grieved that Matadormus did not stay, for he greatly loved him. Turning to the apostles, he said that it was as easy for a camel to go through the needle’s eye as for self-satisfied rich men to enter the kingdom. Peter, astonished, asked: “⟦Q 163:3.2⟧Who then, Lord, can be saved?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered: “⟦Q 163:3.2⟧No, Peter, but all who put their trust in riches shall hardly enter into the spiritual life that leads to eternal progress. But even then, much which is impossible to man is not beyond the reach of the Father in heaven; rather should we recognize that with God all things are possible.⟦/Q⟧” And when Peter said they had left everything to follow him, Jesus promised that whoever had left home or family for the kingdom would receive manifold more in this world, with persecutions, and in the world to come eternal life. Then he told of the householder who hired laborers at dawn, at nine, at noon, at three, and at five in the afternoon, and paid every man a denarius. To those who grumbled, the householder said: “⟦Q 163:3.7⟧My friends, I do you no wrong. Did not each of you agree to work for a denarius a day?… Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with my own? or do you begrudge my generosity because I desire to be good and to show mercy?⟦/Q⟧”
ch39.b012: On Tuesday, December 6, the whole company of almost three hundred broke camp and moved to the Jordan near Pella, to the very spring where John the Baptist had camped years before. As the new camp was being set up, Jesus took Nathaniel and Thomas and went secretly up to Jerusalem for the feast of the dedication. When the two apostles realized where he was going, they pleaded with him with every argument they could find, but to all their warnings he answered only: “⟦Q 164:0.1⟧I would give these teachers in Israel another opportunity to see the light, before my hour comes.⟦/Q⟧”
ch39.b013: They reached Jericho in the late afternoon and lodged there, and that evening a considerable company gathered to ask questions. A certain lawyer, hoping to entangle Jesus, asked what he should do to inherit eternal life. Jesus asked him what was written in the law, and the lawyer answered: “⟦Q 164:1.1⟧To love the Lord God with all your heart, soul, mind, and strength, and your neighbor as yourself.⟦/Q⟧” “You have answered right,” said Jesus; “⟦Q 164:1.1⟧this, if you really do, will lead to life everlasting.⟦/Q⟧” But the lawyer, wishing to justify himself and to embarrass Jesus, drew closer and asked: “⟦Q 164:1.2⟧But, Teacher, I should like you to tell me just who is my neighbor?⟦/Q⟧” The law defined one’s neighbor as “the children of one’s people,” and the lawyer hoped to draw from Jesus some statement that could be called an attack on the sacred law.
ch39.b014: Jesus discerned his motive and told a story any Jericho audience would understand. “⟦Q 164:1.3⟧A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell into the hands of cruel brigands, who robbed him, stripped him and beat him, and departing, left him half dead.⟦/Q⟧” A priest came that way and passed by on the other side; so did a Levite. “⟦Q 164:1.3⟧Now, about this time, a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed down to Jericho, came across this wounded man; and when he saw how he had been robbed and beaten, he was moved with compassion, and going over to him, he bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine, and setting the man upon his own beast, brought him here to the inn and took care of him. And on the morrow he took out some money and, giving it to the host, said: ‘Take good care of my friend, and if the expense is more, when I come back again, I will repay you.’ Now let me ask you: Which of these three turned out to be the neighbor of him who fell among the robbers?⟦/Q⟧” The lawyer saw that he had fallen into his own snare, and, unwilling even to speak that odious word Samaritan, he answered, “⟦Q 164:1.3⟧He who showed mercy on him.⟦/Q⟧” And Jesus said, “Go and do likewise.”
ch39.b015: Josiah and the Pool of Siloam
ch39.b016: On Friday night some twenty-five Jewish leaders who believed Jesus’ teaching met with him at the house of Nicodemus, among them Eber, Matadormus, and Joseph of Arimathea. Both they and the two apostles were amazed at the breadth and depth of the Master’s remarks. They offered plans for winning the rest of the Sanhedrin, and Jesus listened silently, knowing that none of them would work.
ch39.b017: On the Sabbath morning, as Jesus and the two apostles drew near the temple, they passed a well-known beggar who had been born blind, sitting in his usual place. Jesus paused and looked at him, and Nathaniel asked: “⟦Q 164:3.2⟧Master, who did sin, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?⟦/Q⟧” The rabbis taught that such blindness came from sin. Jesus answered: “⟦Q 164:3.7⟧Neither did this man sin nor his parents that the works of God might be manifest in him. This blindness has come upon him in the natural course of events, but we must now do the works of Him who sent me, while it is still day.⟦/Q⟧” Then, stooping, he spat on the ground and mixed the clay with the spittle, put it on the man’s sightless eyes, and said: “⟦Q 164:3.8⟧Go, my son, wash away this clay in the pool of Siloam, and immediately you shall receive your sight.⟦/Q⟧” Josiah did so, and came back seeing. He had not asked to be healed, and he did not even know who his benefactor was. Jesus did this on the Sabbath, near the temple, as an open challenge to the Sanhedrin.
ch39.b018: By midafternoon the talk around the temple was such that the Sanhedrin convened, breaking its own rule against meeting on the Sabbath. They feared to summon Jesus, so they sent for Josiah. An older Pharisee declared that a man who broke the Sabbath could not be from God; a younger member who secretly believed asked how a sinner could do such things, and a serious division arose. They called Josiah’s parents, but the poor, frightened couple, knowing that believers were being cast out of the synagogue, said only: “⟦Q 164:4.7⟧We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind, but how it is that he has come to see, or who it was that opened his eyes, we know not. Ask him; he is of age; let him speak for himself.⟦/Q⟧”
ch39.b019: They called Josiah again and pressed him to give God the glory and admit that the man was a sinner. But Josiah was neither dumb nor lacking in humor: “⟦Q 164:4.9⟧Whether this man is a sinner, I know not; but one thing I do know—that, whereas I was blind, now I see.⟦/Q⟧” When they kept questioning him, he answered impatiently: “⟦Q 164:4.10⟧I have told you exactly how it all happened, and if you did not believe my testimony, why would you hear it again? Would you by any chance also become his disciples?⟦/Q⟧” The council broke up in confusion, almost violence. “We are disciples of Moses,” the leaders cried, “⟦Q 164:4.10⟧but as for this man Jesus, we know not whence he is.⟦/Q⟧” Josiah climbed upon a stool and shouted that here was a great marvel, that they did not know whence this man was, yet he had opened the eyes of one born blind, a thing unheard of since the beginning of the world. “⟦Q 164:4.11⟧I tell you, if this man were not from God, he could not do this.⟦/Q⟧” They went at once to cast him out of the synagogue. Josiah had entered the trial knowing little of Jesus; his bold testimony grew in his mind as the unjust proceedings went on.
ch39.b020: Meanwhile Jesus was teaching close by in Solomon’s Porch, where the people sheltered from the winter weather. When some demanded that he say plainly whether he was the Messiah, he answered: “⟦Q 164:5.2⟧My sheep hear my voice and I know them and they follow me. And to all who follow my teaching I give eternal life; they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand.… The Father and I are one.⟦/Q⟧” Some ran for stones, and he passed out of the temple precincts. When he heard that Josiah had been cast out, he went to his house and said: “⟦Q 164:5.4⟧Josiah, do you believe in the Son of God?⟦/Q⟧” Josiah answered, “⟦Q 164:5.4⟧Tell me who he is that I may believe in him.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said: “⟦Q 164:5.4⟧You have both seen and heard him, and it is he who now speaks to you.⟦/Q⟧” And Josiah said, “Lord, I believe,” and falling down, he worshiped. He went with them to Pella and became a lifelong preacher of the gospel of the kingdom.
ch39.b022: More than three hundred Jerusalemites, Pharisees and others, followed Jesus north to Pella, and one evening, in their hearing and that of the twelve, he spoke of the true shepherd, who enters the fold by the door and whose voice the sheep know and follow, while they flee from a stranger. Then he said: “⟦Q 165:2.7,165:2.8⟧I will declare that I am both the door to the Father’s sheepfold and at the same time the true shepherd of my Father’s flocks.… The thief breaks into the fold only to steal, and to kill, and to destroy; but I have come that you all may have life and have it more abundantly.⟦/Q⟧” The hireling flees when the wolf comes, but the true shepherd lays down his life for the sheep. “⟦Q 165:2.9,165:2.10⟧But I have many other sheep not of this fold, and these words are true not only of this world.… But, mind you, if I lay down my life, I will take it up again. No man nor any other creature can take away my life.⟦/Q⟧” The Pharisees went out into the night, saying, “⟦Q 165:2.11⟧He is either mad or has a devil.⟦/Q⟧” But on the morrow about half of those Jewish teachers professed belief in him.
ch39.b023: On Friday, December 30, the seventy came back two by two to the Pella camp, with many believers, and the evening meal was delayed more than an hour while they told their experiences. When they said that even the devils had been subject to them, Jesus said: “⟦Q 163:6.2⟧It is not strange that these disobedient minor spirits should be subject to you, seeing that I beheld Satan falling as lightning from heaven. But rejoice not so much over this.… but the rather rejoice that your names are written on the rolls of heaven.⟦/Q⟧” At last he could see men going out to spread the good news without his presence. The next day he warned the seventy against the subtleties of spiritual pride and said: “⟦Q 163:6.7⟧I always stand near, and my invitation-call is, and ever shall be, Come to me all you who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.⟦/Q⟧”
ch39.b025: On Tuesday, January 3, A.D. 30, Abner sent the seventy out to the cities and villages of Perea, the last mission of the Master’s life, lasting almost three months. There were no miracles; the women’s corps, now sixty-two strong, took over most of the care of the sick. By mid-January more than twelve hundred people were gathered at Pella, and by mid-March over four thousand.
ch39.b026: On the Sabbath, January 28, Jesus spoke to almost three thousand: “⟦Q 165:3.4⟧Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies?… I say to you: Fear not; you are of much more value than many sparrows.⟦/Q⟧” Afterward, while the apostles baptized in the river, a young man asked Jesus to make his brother divide their inheritance with him. Jesus said: “⟦Q 165:4.1⟧Man, who made me a divider over you?⟦/Q⟧” and warned all to keep free from covetousness, telling of the rich man who pulled down his barns to build greater ones, said to his soul, “Take now your ease,” and that very night lost his life. When another asked whether it was a sin to possess honest wealth, Jesus answered that it was not, provided one’s treasure was in heaven, “⟦Q 165:4.5,165:4.6⟧for where your treasure is there will your heart be also.… Fail not to recognize the danger of wealth’s becoming, not your servant, but your master.⟦/Q⟧”
ch39.b027: That evening he told the twelve not to be anxious about food or raiment: “⟦Q 165:5.2⟧Consider the ravens.… Which of you by anxiety can add a handbreadth to your stature or a day to your life?⟦/Q⟧” But hard trials lay ahead. “⟦Q 165:5.5,165:5.6⟧Every one of you, gird up the loins of your minds and let your lamps be kept burning. Keep yourselves like men who are watching for their master to return from the marriage feast.… Be you also on watch for yourselves, for in an hour that you least suspect and in a manner you think not, shall the Son of Man depart.⟦/Q⟧” For some minutes the twelve sat in silence.
